newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp seen relaunching Thyssen bid.
newsitem.headline: Krupp seen relaunching Thyssen bid.

text.p: German steel group Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp plans to relaunch a hostile takeover bid for rival Thyssen AG the week after Easter, according to the early edition of Saturday's Die Welt daily distributed late on Friday.
Citing reliable sources, it said Krupp believed Thyssen had only agreed to talks this week about a merger of their steel companies in order to win time to defend itself against a complete takeover.
"But Krupp wants a complete merger," the newspaper wrote.
Krupp launched a rare hostile takeover of its larger rival Thyssen earlier this week, offering shareholders 435 marks ($257) a share, a 25 percent premium over the previous day's share price.

The move sparked spontaneous work stoppages by thousands of steel workers in the Ruhr valley industry heartland and local politicians intervened, persuading the two companies to begin talks over a merger of just their steel companies.

Such a merger would create one of the world's largest steel operations, but Krupp has said the full merger of the two companies would create huge cost savings in other areas as well, such as engineering and automotive components.
Citing consultant sources, the newspaper report said Krupp expects annual savings of at least one billion marks in the event of complete merger with Thyssen.
According to the newspaper report, Krupp has secured sufficient bank financing for its offer and to counter potential defensive tactics by Thyssen.
One such move could be a decision by Thyssen to carry out an already-approved capital increase of 350 million marks. That would raise the costs for Krupp by around three billion marks.
Krupp has secured bank financing of 15 billion marks in the event that it has to acquire 100 percent of Thyssen's capital.

The newspaper said that Krupp's steel merger plan would convert its traditional blast furnace operations in Dortmund to a modern electric steel plant, thereby cutting 1,500 jobs. But these job cuts would be carried out without lay-offs. ($1=1.6920 Mark)
